slots.text: Most founders validate ideas by asking "would you use this?" Wrong question. Ask "what did you do the last 3 times this problem happened?" Their actual behavior tells the real story.

3 signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything you show them
2. They ask when it'll be "enterprise ready"
3. They want to "hop on a call to discuss partnership opportunities"

Find people who hate their current solution.
AI tools work best when they remove steps from existing workflows, not when they try to create entirely new ones. People don't want to learn new habits. They want old habits to work better.
The hardest part about user interviews isn't getting people to talk. It's shutting up long enough to hear what they're actually saying instead of what confirms your assumptions.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes it's the only thing preventing users from making mistakes they'll regret. Remove the right friction, keep the guardrails.

4 workflow questions that actually matter:

1. What breaks first when you're busy?
2. What do you redo most often?
3. What requires the most back-and-forth?
4. What do you procrastinate on?

That's where the real problems live.
Most validation conversations fail because founders ask what people want instead of watching what they actually do. Behavior beats opinions every time.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:
1. They love everything you show them
2. They have lots of time to chat
3. They ask when it'll be free
4. They suggest features for someone else's use case
The AI tools that actually stick in my workflow are the boring ones that eliminate 30 seconds of friction 50 times a day. The flashy demos everyone shares usually solve problems I don't have.
Founders who validate ideas by building landing pages get signups. Founders who validate by finding existing broken workflows get customers.
User interviews are pattern recognition disguised as conversation. Stop after you can predict what the next three people will say.

Workflow friction usually hides in:
1. Handoffs between people
2. Copy-paste between tools
3. Context switching
4. Waiting for approvals
5. Manual status updates
Most founders skip validation because they think they already know their users. The ones who actually talk to strangers before building anything have an unfair advantage.

3 things that kill user interviews:

1. Leading questions ("Would you use this?")
2. Talking more than listening
3. Only interviewing people who already like you

The uncomfortable conversations are the valuable ones.
Been thinking about why AI tools feel clunky in real workflows. It's not the AI that's the problem - it's that we're adding steps instead of removing them. Good AI should make you forget it exists.
Founders who validate ideas quickly tend to have one thing in common: they're comfortable being wrong. The ones who take months to "perfect" their hypothesis usually never ship.
Friction isn't always bad. Sometimes the extra step is what makes people value what they're getting. The trick is knowing which friction to remove and which to keep.

Signs your idea validation is actually working:

1. People interrupt you with their problems
2. They ask when it's ready without you prompting
3. Conversations go longer than planned
4. They connect you with others who have the same pain
Most founders skip user interviews because they're afraid of hearing their idea sucks. But the real fear should be building something nobody wants for 6 months.

3 signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:
1. You only talk to friends who are too nice to crush your dreams
2. You're asking leading questions
3. You mistake polite interest for buying intent

The hardest part about building with AI isn't the technical integration. It's figuring out which parts of your workflow actually need to be automated vs which parts users want to control. Most founders automate the wrong things.
Every founder thinks their signup flow is simple until they watch someone try to use it. The number of clicks isn't the problem. It's the number of decisions you're forcing them to make.
User feedback falls into two buckets: what they say they want and what they actually pay for. Only the second one matters for your roadmap.

4 friction points that kill conversion but founders never notice:
1. Asking for a credit card before showing value
2. Multi-step onboarding for simple products
3. Industry jargon in your copy
4. Making users think about pricing tiers
Most founders skip validation because they're afraid their idea isn't special. But ideas are cheap. Execution on a validated problem is what matters.

Signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love everything you show them
2. They ask about features, not problems
3. They want to "think about it"
4. They suggest pivoting to their industry
Building AI features feels backwards right now. You start with the capability, then hunt for the use case. But users don't care about your model - they care about their workflow getting easier.
The best product feedback comes from users who are almost angry about their current solution. Mild frustration doesn't convert. Rage does.

Workflow friction always hides in the same places:

1. Context switching between tools
2. Manual data entry that could be automated
3. Waiting for someone else's approval
4. Recreating the same thing twice
User interviews are pattern recognition. One person's complaint is an anecdote. Five people saying the same thing is a signal worth building for.
Most founders ask users what features they want. Better question: what are you doing right before you'd use our product? The context matters more than the wishlist.

3 signs your idea validation is actually just confirmation bias:
1. You only talk to people who already agree with you
2. You ask leading questions
3. You ignore the lukewarm responses and focus on the enthusiastic ones

The hardest part of building with AI isn't the technical integration. It's figuring out which parts of your workflow actually benefit from automation vs which parts users want to control themselves. Getting this wrong kills adoption fast.
Users will tolerate 3-4 extra clicks if each step feels obvious. They'll abandon after 1 click if they don't understand what just happened.
When someone says your product is 'interesting' during user interviews, that's usually a polite no. When they ask how much it costs or when it launches, that's a maybe becoming a yes.

4 friction points that kill SaaS products quietly:
1. Signup requires too much upfront info
2. First value moment takes longer than 2 minutes
3. Integration setup needs engineering help
4. Cancellation requires talking to sales
Most founders think they need to validate their solution. Wrong order. You need to validate that the problem actually causes people to change their behavior.

3 signs you're talking to the wrong users:

1. They love your idea but won't commit to using it
2. They keep suggesting features for other people
3. They're more excited about it than you expected

The AI tooling paradox: we can build faster than ever, but we're also building more things that don't matter. Speed amplifies both good and bad judgment. The constraint was never technical capability.
Teams that obsess over removing friction from their own workflows ship products with better UX. Internal pain tolerance directly correlates with what you'll subject users to.
User interviews aren't about asking people what they want. They're about understanding what they currently do when the problem shows up.

4 workflow friction points that kill momentum:

1. Context switching between tools
2. Manual data entry that could be automated
3. Waiting for approvals on obvious decisions
4. Rebuilding the same thing twice
